Treasury Financing Operations
January Certificate Maturity

A one-year issue of 7/8 percent certificates of indebtedness outstanding in the amount of $3,174 million matured on January 1, 1948. On December 19, 1947, the Secretary of the Treasury announced the offering of a new 12-month 1-1/8 percent certificate of indebtedness in exchange, par for par, for the maturing certificates. Cash subscriptions were not received. The new certificates are dated January 1, 1948, and bear interest from that date at the rate of 1-1/8 percent per annum. Interest will be paid in full with the principal on the maturity date, January 1, 1949. The certificates were issued in bearer form only, in denominations of $1,000, $5,000, $10,000, $100,000, and $1,000,000.

Reports to the Treasury on the ownership of Government securities indicate that on November 30, 1947, about 66 percent of the $3,134 million of certificates maturing January 1, 1948, were owned by commercial banks and Federal Reserve Banks. The ownership figures for November 30 are the latest which are available for holdings of both commercial banks and Federal Reserve Banks.

Subscription books were opened on December 19, and were closed at the close of business on December 27. Four hundred million dollars of the Federal Reserve Bank holdings of the maturing certificates of indebtedness were redeemed for cash. Exchange subscriptions for the new issue amounted to $2,592 million, leaving $142 million to be paid in cash to holders other than Federal Reserve Banks.
Treasury Bills Retired and Refunded in December

Additional reductions in Treasury bills outstanding were made in the first two weeks of December. The four issues maturing weekly during the month totaled $5.0 billion and the total refunded was $4.8 billion. Each of the first two maturing issues was reduced by $100 million.

first three maturities were for $1.3 billion each, and the fourth for $1.1 billion. Bill retirements from April 17, 1947, when the first bill reduction was made, through December 26 have totaled $1.9 billion. The average rates of discount for the four December offerings, beginning with that dated December 4, were 0.944 percent, 0.948 percent, 0.949 percent, and 0.951 percent, respectively.
Reinvestment of Proceeds of Maturing Savings Bonds

Announcement was made by the Treasury Department on December 31, 1947, that in furtherance of the campaign to increase the sale of savings bonds, individual holders of Series C-1938 savings bonds, which started to mature January 1, 1948, would be permitted to reinvest the proceeds, as they mature, in Series E savings bonds currently on sale, without regard to the $5,000 (maturity value) annual limitation on E bond holdings. Since Series E bonds may be purchased only in the names of individuals, only those Series C-1938 savings bonds held by individuals are eligible for this privilege.

Any issuing agent qualified to cash savings bonds can accomplish this exchange by redeeming matured bonds and applying the proceeds to the purchase of new Series E bonds. Holders are permitted to reinvest any part of the proceeds of their maturing bonds to the extent of such denominational amount as the proceeds fully cover. The bonds may be exchanged also, of course, at any Federal Reserve Bank or branch, or at the Treasury Department.

The new bonds will be dated as of the first day of the month in which the matured Series C-1935 savings bonds are presented for payment. In order to preserve the continuity of the investment, holders of the maturing bonds should present them for exchange during the month in which they mature.

Treasury Bulletin
Capital Movements Between the United States and Foreign Countries, and Net Position in Foreign Currencies

This chapter on Capital Movements between the United States and Foreign Countries and Position in Foreign Currencies is divided into four main groups. Section I of Capital Movements, the Historical Summary, contains data regarding capital movements by the principal types of data, and by years from 1935, and currently by months. Each type of data is then broken down into its chief components in the same chronological detail.

Section II supplies a geographic breakdown by principal countries on a monthly basis. The total capital movements are given first and then the principal categories are shown separately. In addition, at this point, the total outstanding claims on and liabilities to foreign countries are each presented.
Details with respect to capital movements and short-term claims and liabilities are presented in Section III as of the latest month for which the data are available.
The last group contains monthly data regarding the
net position in foreign currencies of United States banks and brokers, their outstanding foreign exchange contracts, and purchases and sales of foreign exchange, both spot and forward.

These data are based on reports filed each month by banks, bankers, and brokers throughout the United States. The reports are collected, checked, and tabulated by the twelve Federal Reserve Banks. The totals are then forwarded to the Treasury Department for consolidation and publication.
Figures for previous periods may be obtained from the following sources:
